This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
At a midterm campaign rally in Montana last night, President Trump spoke of plans for a new military range to test advanced weapons.
>> I'm pleased to inform you and announce that right here in Montana,
the Department of War is going to establish a new super range for testing advanced weapons and technologies,
including potential autonomous weapons, space and electronic warfare technology,
supersonics and hypersonics.
>> Trump was in Kalispell, Montana outside Glacier National Park, his second stop of the day,
and part of a tour of western states supporting Republican candidates out of the November 3rd midterm elections.
California lawmakers say a surge in immigration raids in the state could suppress the vote come November,
Anthony Victoria with member station KVCR reports.
>> Secretary of State Shirley Weber condemned the immigration raids in a video conference with reporters.
Weber said there's no question that the raids will scare people away from the polls.
>> People feel that ICE is waiting for individuals who look a little different.
We see every day someone being attacked, someone being stopped.
>> DHS has launched enforcement campaigns in San Diego, the Inland Empire,
which is outside of Los Angeles, and the Central Valley,
where the Latino vote will be decisive in a high profile race to flip a congressional district from red to blue.
Weber encouraged people who are afraid to go to the polls to vote by mail.
For NPR News, I'm Anthony Victoria in Riverside, California.
>> Learning more about the circumstances surrounding Krista Pike's botched execution attempt in Tennessee last month.
Pike was given two rounds of lethal injection drugs,
but when she survived, an hour and a half had passed before the death row inmate was taken to the hospital.
Catherine Sweeney of member station WPLN reports on 911 recordings, which are offering new details from that night.
>> No one has ever survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs.
So, Tennessee's execution protocols had no guidance.
Recordings obtained by WPLN depict a communication breakdown
that found dispatchers trying to figure out if requests for help were prank calls.
Prison workers denied needing medical help several times,
even after an ambulance, fire trucks, and police escorts were sent out.
Here's a short exchange.
>> We have responders that are standing by and we're just trying to verify.
I'm being told that nobody from our facility called you.
>> Pike was eventually taken to a hospital and has since been released back to prison.
For NPR News, I'm Catherine Sweeney in Nashville.
>> Now to northwestern Pakistan, where rescuers are working to reach several children reported trapped beneath the rubble of a roof collapse.
The collapse happened at a private school.
Officials say at least 10 children were killed and more than two dozen others injured.
And you're listening to NPR News.
The Justice Department is threatening legal action against the state of California.
The DOJ sent a letter this week to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber,
saying it has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive
with a list of names of people the federal government alleges are likely non-citizens
who have received mail ballots for next month's midterm elections.
The letter gives the state 48 hours to review the list and wants those ballots set aside
until citizen questions are resolved.
If not, the DOJ says it will sue.
However, judges have dismissed dozens of election-related demands made by DOJ during President Trump's second term.
Scientists say elephants have an outsized impact on landscapes both in life and death, as Solana Gordon reports.
>> Elephants are ecosystem engineers.
They knock down trees, they disperse seeds, but scientists in South Africa's Kruger National Park
found something they didn't expect after the animals die.
The group monitored dozens of elephant carcasses on the savannah
and found that over time the remains created unique nutrient-rich hotspots for certain grasses.
This drew animals like zebras and antelope well after any visual signs of the elephant had disappeared.
Courtney Reed is with UC Santa Barbara in Princeton.
She led the research.
>> Seeing that even like eight years on, you have all of these different herbivores that live on the savannah
that are really selecting for those nitrogen-rich grasses.
It was just exciting.
>> Reed says this lasting legacy highlights the importance of elephants as they face threats of extinction.
The findings were published in the proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Alana Gordon, NPR News.
>> And I'm Joel Snyder.
